paper.1 Introduction: The current Theorem 1.1 begins with a nonzero smooth recurrent similarity profile and constructs finite-time solutions with quantitative blow-up and profile-error estimates. The linked whole-space and periodic implications instead conclude nonexistence of a global smooth solution in specified classes. Their profile premise adds second-derivative and pressure-gradient decay; Remark 1.2 explicitly supplies only the extra velocity regularity. The periodic excluded class allows nonperiodic pressure. The certificate implication belongs to an earlier rectangular formulation and remains conditional on its estimates. Read each comparison as a statement about the particular linked assertion: a definition of a target is not a proof of it, and an implication from certificate bounds is not a supplied numerical certificate.
paper.2 Outline of the proof: The whole-space construction represents $\dot H^1_{\rm div}$ by weighted Fourier states, reconstructs $L^6$ velocities and formulates Navier–Stokes through a Bochner integral equation. The transfer assertion chooses a nearby datum in each dense linear subspace and gives a decaying rescaled error. It does not retain Proposition 2.1’s conclusion for every prescribed nearby datum or its fixed finite-dimensional correction space. The regularity theorem works on closed time intervals and gives an unspecified energy bound there, without stating energy nonincrease or one bound on the full half-open lifespan. The periodic target records an unbounded mild curve in the inhomogeneous, possibly nonzero-mean, unit-torus $H^1$ space; the quantitative rates and local profile comparison of Proposition 2.2 are absent from that target.
paper.3 Preliminaries: The formal development constructs the solenoidal homogeneous $H^1$ space through gradient-weighted Fourier classes, establishes heat and dilation laws and the bilinear estimate, and proves the Duhamel continuity, restart and uniqueness results used later. Its compactness theorem is stated first for first inputs in the linear span of smooth compactly supported solenoidal fields, a dense class. Its weak-to-mild implication assumes smooth decaying slices and $L^2$-continuous differences, unlike Lemma 3.6. On the torus it uses an inhomogeneous $H^1$ space of period one with unrestricted mean; the bilinear bound is stated for $0<\tau\le1$. These differences must be retained when comparing with the paper’s homogeneous mean-zero spaces at arbitrary period. A numbered display may combine several clauses, and a theorem proving one clause does not establish the entire display.
paper.4 The equation linearized about $u^*$: The formal development represents the profile in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}$ and works on short rescaled time intervals. Its interval linearization has a genuine inverse once the interaction norm is at most $1/4$; the product over a similarity period differs compactly from a free operator of norm at most $e^{-S/4}$. A real finite-rank spectral splitting, a lift into a dense class of data and a normalized forced recurrence then provide a bounded right inverse for the sequence of interval equations. The nonlinear correction is also stated for such sequences, with endpoint matching and separate residual and datum bounds. The paper presents these constructions on the global weighted spaces $C_\kappa([0,1);X)$. The linked formal statements do not themselves state all of the paper's global weighted estimates, the change from a global source to the forcing of Lemma 4.6, or the identification of the short-interval product with the unsplit trajectory. Those correspondences must be checked separately. The profile-to-orbit step assumes decay through two spatial derivatives and of the pressure gradient, beyond the displayed assumptions (1.3).
paper.5 Blow-up on $\\mathbb R^3$: The formal development constructs a solenoidal cutoff through the radial vector potential and proves the support and inner-agreement properties used in §5. Its estimates are stated for a fixed cutoff about $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$, then rescaled to similarity coordinates: the outer radius is $1/(8\sqrt{T-t})$. The squared $L^2$ bound has linear growth in that radius for $0<T-t\le1$, while the exported gradient-error conclusion is qualitative smallness as $T-t\to0$; it does not retain the paper’s uniform $Cr^{-1/2}$ estimate for every independent physical radius. The physical profile is proved mild on $[0,1)$ from its similarity-time mild equation. Correction is carried out through a sequence of interval equations. The final transfer assertion selects a nearby datum in any prescribed dense linear subspace and gives convergence to the profile after similarity rescaling; its quantifiers do not retain Proposition 2.1’s conclusion for every prescribed nearby datum with one correction space and uniform constants.
paper.6 Blow-up on the torus: The formal construction starts on the unit torus with the inhomogeneous solenoidal $H^1$ norm and permits a nonzero mean. The paper first works on a torus of period $L$ with the mean-zero homogeneous norm. Accordingly, the formal transplant identity contains the additional term $\mu\|g\|_2^2$. Time is divided into intervals with scales $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$; the cutoff residual and correction are estimated in supremum norms on the normalized intervals. Local restriction records three $L^2$ derivative entries and an $L^6$ value entry in a maximum norm, allowing tuples without derivative compatibility. The heat comparisons yield arbitrarily small errors for sufficiently small scale on the specified compact time ranges, without the explicit powers of $L$ in Lemma 6.1. Two localized operator comparisons transfer an exact right inverse, after which the corrected intervals are joined. The final mild-solution assertion retains smooth periodic initial data and finite-time unboundedness of the periodic norm; it does not state Proposition 2.2’s two-sided blow-up rate or local estimate relative to the self-similar profile.
paper.7 From a certificate to a profile: Section 7 assumes approximate profiles, forcing and constraint fields, and quantitative estimates, then derives a weak profile. The formal development represents the velocities in homogeneous Sobolev spaces and the forcing over a normalized period in $L^2$; weak equations use solenoidal test fields. Its certificate asks for global joint $C^1$ dependence on parameter, time and space, supplied weak Hessians and operator-norm decay bounds, and it permits $m=1$ when the paper selects $m=2$. The parameter argument solves the nonlinear correction at each parameter and then uses a finite-dimensional fixed point, whereas the paper uses a joint weak-topology fixed point. The final existence implications do not retain all the information in Theorem 7.1: the selected parameter, quantitative approximation, specified period, identity twist and full prescribed symmetry set are not all part of their conclusions. These implications remain conditional on the certificate hypotheses.
paper.Appendix A Proofs of the lemmas of Secti: The formal development proves the abstract mild-solution estimates for a strongly continuous contraction semigroup and a symmetric bilinear operator with the bound $C\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$, including integrability and continuity of Duhamel terms, restarting and uniqueness. Its uniqueness proof uses short intervals; the paper's proof uses an exponentially weighted norm. In the whole-space realization, a continuous mild curve from smooth compactly supported solenoidal data has smooth velocity and pressure on each closed finite time interval, with the momentum equation stated on its interior and equality to the given velocity at every time almost everywhere in space. This statement gives a finite energy bound on the interval; it does not state the energy nonincrease printed in Lemma 2.3. The linked torus results use the unit torus with inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm and allow the constant mode; the paper's corresponding estimates use the zero-mean homogeneous space and arbitrary spatial period.
paper.Appendix B Certificates in the formaliza: Appendix B specifies finite representations and conditions sufficient for a certificate. The formal development derives regularity and weak derivatives from the representation, proves multiplier and cell implications, treats unresolved harmonics and exterior regions, and assembles finite-dimensional matrix inequalities. The remaining profile-change, adjoint and offset estimates reduce to specified norm and pairing budgets. A finite representation does not itself verify those budgets: pointwise bounds, integral bounds, positive pivot conditions and matrix comparisons remain assumptions. Some auxiliary statements use broader classes and everywhere-defined derivatives or integrals; for these, the conventions and the separate hypotheses that justify the usual analytic interpretation must be stated. The final cell theorem assumes all fifteen groups of conditions and concludes nonexistence of global smooth solutions in the stated whole-space energy class and for periodic velocity on the unit torus. It supplies no numerical certificate satisfying the conditions.
paper.Appendix C The computation of the approx: The linked formal statements describe classes of finite harmonic fields, their radial phases, symmetry and joining conditions, and algebraic or continuum identities used in the linearized equation. They also describe admissible forcing modes and multiplier weights. These are conditions on supplied fields and numbers. They do not carry out the continuation, Newton iteration, flexible GMRES solves, mesh refinement or optimization reported in Appendix C, and they do not supply the particular field with $\varkappa=19$ and $\bar S\approx0.36$. The harmonic label must be converted to its time and azimuthal frequencies before comparing rotating-frame formulas; the radial phase also has a rate parameter whose normalization must be matched. The formalization contains the conditional reductions from certificate data, while the numerical certificate and the rigorous computation verifying its inequalities are absent.

statement_files.lean/Challenge.lean: This file states the unforced Navier–Stokes equations, the smooth and weak recurrent profile hypotheses and their global-nonexistence consequences: the smooth hypothesis gives both the whole-space and the periodic conclusion, and the weak hypothesis gives the whole-space conclusion. It uses functions on ℝ³ for both the whole space and the periodic problem. The whole-space conclusion excludes global smooth solutions with uniformly bounded kinetic energy; the periodic conclusion excludes periodic velocities even when the pressure is merely smooth. These conclusions omit the singular time, rates and profile approximation of Theorem 1.1. The smooth-profile hypothesis includes explicit Hessian and pressure-gradient decay beyond the bounds displayed in (1.3). Each of these points needs its own comparison with the paper.
statement_files.lean/CertificateChallenge.lean: This file gives an earlier sufficient certificate with a translated parameter box, a norm restricted to a ball and a slope-inverse inclusion argument. It defines the weak perturbation class and the period and spatial energies used later. Its approximate profile is jointly C² with Hessian decay, and its force weight is one. These requirements differ from the row and adjoint construction in §§7.2–7.3. The final implication assumes that all earlier certificate conditions hold and concludes a nonzero weak recurrent profile; it does not supply numerical data or the additional outputs of Theorem 7.1.
statement_files.lean/ExtendedCertificateChallenge.lean: This file states the certificate corresponding to §§7.2–7.3: the interval-and-ellipsoid parameter set, a separate reference profile, orthonormal rows with separate nonnegative weights, residual estimates and adjoint inclusion bounds. It represents the pressure gradient by a vector field annihilating solenoidal tests. Its assumptions include global C¹ parameter dependence, pointwise decay of a supplied weak Hessian and uniform-in-time spatial L² adjoint bounds, which are stronger than the displayed assumptions in the paper; it also requires c₂≥0, whereas (7.18) allows any real c₂. Two implications preserve the conditions under normalization of the force weight and transfer from the reference to the approximate profile. Existence of data satisfying the complete conditions gives a weak recurrent profile.
statement_files.lean/CoerciveChallenge.lean: This file states the multiplier estimates behind Proposition B.1 and Lemma B.2, first in the earlier certificate format and then with finite curl and velocity pieces. It states the rotating-frame averages, the conversion weights, the five modal terms, the separate positive and negative contributions, and the hypotheses for passing from multiplier bounds to coercivity. The raw time-angle pair is (2ι₂−ι₁,ϰι₁) for the paper’s label ι. The coefficient c remains general until it is set to 3/50. Several admissibility statements allow a wider class of functions than the prescribed polynomial representations in Appendix B. Full multiplier-piece error coefficients are explicit in the source but not printed in the paper.
statement_files.lean/ExtendedCoerciveChallenge.lean: This file extends the multiplier argument to C¹ reference fields with a supplied weak Hessian and separates the multiplier construction, smooth approximation, limit passage and absorption statements. It then includes the row terms of the extended certificate. The coercive estimate follows after an all-perturbation lower bound corresponding to (B.21) is assumed, together with the stated admissibility and constant inequalities. The algebraic implications can be stated without row orthogonality; the intended seminorm interpretation requires it. Equalities obtained by substituting the ordinary Hessian are distinguished from analytic statements identifying it with a weak Hessian.
statement_files.lean/CellLayerChallenge.lean: This file expresses the conditions of Appendix B through finite harmonics, polynomial and Hermite representations, cells, traces, local quadratic forms, error bounds and matrix inequalities arranged in a tree. It also contains an earlier steady fractional variant, which is identified separately. The classical assembly fixes c=3/50, w*=39/50 and the constraint weight 1000, relates the finite row and adjoint constructions to the extended certificate, and concludes the whole-space and periodic-velocity nonexistence statements. Its conditions still quantify over entire cells, exterior regions, parameters and perturbations. The final theorem assumes all these conditions; supplying the data alone produces no numerical certificate.
